\chapter{Good Afternoon}
\label{ch:la-good-afternoon}

This chapter is generated from the canonical micro-lessons used by Language Ladder.

\section[salvē (post merīdiem)]{salvē (post merīdiem) — the one that isn't there}

\label{lesson:LA-C36-salve-post-meridiem}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Three lessons in a row, you've met a modern phrase built on real (if sometimes invisible) Latin grammar for "good \_\_\_." This lesson is different: there's honestly nothing to build.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Bonam noctem}, \textbf{bonum māne}, and \textbf{bonum vesperum} are all modern, pedagogical phrases — not classically attested — but each pairs \emph{bonus} directly with a \textbf{single noun} in the accusative: \emph{noctem}, \emph{māne}, \emph{vesperum}. "Good afternoon" can't take that same shape, because you already learned last lesson that Latin has \textbf{no simplex noun} for "afternoon" at all — there's no \emph{afternoonem} for \emph{bonus} to modify. \textbf{Bonum post merīdiem} doesn't work: \emph{post merīdiem} ("after noon") is a whole \textbf{prepositional phrase}, not a noun, so \emph{bonus} has nothing to agree with. A three-word workaround, \textbf{bonum tempus pōmerīdiānum} ("good afternoon time"), actually \textbf{is} grammatical — \emph{pōmerīdiānus} ("of the afternoon") is a real word Cicero himself uses, and here \emph{bonus} agrees with a genuine noun, \emph{tempus} ("time"). But it's a \textbf{periphrasis}, not a direct two-word match for the other three phrases — and it isn't itself attested anywhere as something Romans actually said as a greeting.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: why "bonum post merīdiem" doesn't work — no noun for bonus to agree with; why "bonum tempus pōmerīdiānum" DOES work, but isn't attested as a real greeting{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the grammatical adjective — pōmerīdiānum, "of the afternoon"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Does Latin have a two-word phrase for "good afternoon" the way it has \emph{bonum vesperum} for evening? (\textbf{No} — Latin has no simplex noun for "afternoon" for \emph{bonus} to pair with.) Is there ANY grammatical Latin phrase at all? (\textbf{Yes} — \emph{bonum tempus pōmerīdiānum} is real grammar, but a three-word periphrasis, not attested as an actual greeting.) What did Romans say in the afternoon instead? (\textbf{Salvē} — the same everyday greeting from Chapter 1.) Why doesn't \emph{bonum post merīdiem} work grammatically? (\emph{Post merīdiem} is a whole prepositional phrase, not a single noun \emph{bonus} can agree with.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[salvē / salvēte]{salvē — the greeting that does not watch the clock}

\label{lesson:LA-C36-timeless-salve}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Latin cannot build a neat two-word "good afternoon." What did Romans actually need in that time slot? Nothing beyond a greeting you already know.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Salvē} to one person and \textbf{salvēte} to several people mean "be well." Neither form contains a morning, afternoon, or evening boundary. Romans could use the greeting whenever they met someone.

English encourages a learner to search for four matched clock-based formulas. Latin everyday greetings do not divide the day that way. The missing afternoon formula is therefore not a hole in Roman conversation.

The time-of-day arc now has three different kinds of evidence:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a real institution, the morning \textbf{salūtātiō}
  \item grammatical but modern phrases such as \textbf{bonam noctem}
  \item no dedicated formula at all for afternoon—just \textbf{salvē}
\end{itemize}

Learning those differences is more faithful than forcing four symmetrical translations into Latin.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "salvē" — be well, to one person{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "salvēte" — be well, to several people{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the time restriction — none{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What can one Roman say on meeting another in the afternoon? (\textbf{Salvē.}) What is the plural? (\textbf{Salvēte.}) Do these words encode a time of day? (\textbf{No.}) Why is there no conversational gap? (\textbf{The everyday greeting already works whenever people meet.})
\end{tcolorbox}
